Neighborhood aggregation

Source: vignettes/articles/aggregation.Rmd
aggregation.Rmd

Edges show individual cell pairs. Aggregation summarizes them for each cell’s neighborhood, which gives you per-cell values to compare across a tissue.

library(NICHESv2)
library(data.table)

data(NICHESv2_example)
obj <- aggregate_NICHESObject(
  NICHESv2_example,
  cell.type.col = "celltype",
  verbose = FALSE
)
names(obj$aggregations)
#> [1] "neighborhood.edge.agg"    "neighborhood.composition"

aggregate_NICHESObject() runs add_neighborhood_edge_agg(), then add_neighborhood_composition() if you pass cell.type.col. Each run replaces the previous result.

Edge aggregation

$aggregations$neighborhood.edge.agg has 27 columns, with one row for each (cell, LRM) pair that has signal.

agg <- obj$aggregations$neighborhood.edge.agg
dim(agg)
#> [1] 399  27

Five categories

Each edge in a neighborhood falls into one category relative to the focal cell:

Category Meaning
in A neighbor sends to the focal cell
out The focal cell sends to a neighbor
cross One neighbor sends to another; the focal cell isn’t involved
self.autocrine The focal cell’s own self-loop
other.autocrine A neighbor’s self-loop

The cross category captures what a cell’s surroundings exchange, even when the cell itself takes no part.

Columns

{category} below stands for each of the five categories, or total for all of them together.

Column Meaning
count.{category} Number of edges with signal
score.{category}.sum Total score
score.{category}.mean Total score divided by all edges in the neighborhood, including those with no signal for this LRM
score.{category}.cmean Total score divided by the count, or NA when the count is zero
score.inout.ratio score.in.sum divided by score.out.sum, or NA when nothing is sent

Use mean to compare the overall signal between neighborhoods of different sizes. Use cmean to see how strong the signal is on the edges that carry it.

agg[, .(cell, LRM, count.in, score.in.sum, score.in.mean, score.in.cmean)][1:3]
cell LRM count.in score.in.sum score.in.mean score.in.cmean
Cell_1 Gene11|Gene12 1 10 0.588 10
Cell_1 Gene13|Gene14 0 0 0.000 NA
Cell_1 Gene15|Gene16 0 0 0.000 NA

Edges with no signal for any LR pair still count toward the mean denominator, which comes from $neighborhood.meta$n.edges.

Memory

chunk.size sets how many LR pairs are processed at once, and defaults to 50. Lower it if you run short of memory. Aggregation uses sparse matrix multiplication, so n.cores has no effect on this step.

Neighborhood composition

$aggregations$neighborhood.composition has one row per cell, with counts and proportions of neighboring cell types. By default it counts the focal cell too; pass include.self = FALSE to add_neighborhood_composition() to leave it out.

comp <- obj$aggregations$neighborhood.composition
head(comp[, .(cell, TypeA.neighbor.prop, TypeB.neighbor.prop, TypeC.neighbor.prop)], 3)
cell TypeA.neighbor.prop TypeB.neighbor.prop TypeC.neighbor.prop
Cell_1 1 0 0
Cell_10 1 0 0
Cell_11 1 0 0

This table needs spatial data. In "nonspatial" mode it stops with an error, because neighbor cell types would only reflect the sampling.

Subsets

Aggregate the full object first, then subset. Neighborhood slots and aggregation tables are indexed by cell, so each kept cell keeps its rows unchanged. Those values still describe the cell’s whole neighborhood, including neighbors you didn’t keep.

keep <- obj$cell.meta[celltype == "TypeA", cell]
sub <- obj[keep]

identical(
  sub$aggregations$neighborhood.edge.agg$score.in.sum,
  agg[cell %in% keep]$score.in.sum
)
#> [1] TRUE

The edge slots of a subset keep only edges between kept cells. Two things follow:

  • Summing a cell’s rows in sub$edge.data can give less than its aggregation row.
  • A TissuePlex export of the subset shows only those kept edges.

Recalculating on a subset

The removed edges are gone, so a subset can’t recompute full-tissue values, and trying stops with an error:

add_neighborhood_edge_agg(sub, verbose = FALSE)
#> Error:
#> ! [add_neighborhood_edge_agg] This object is a subset whose neighborhoods include edges to removed cells, so aggregations cannot be recomputed on it. Aggregate the full object before subsetting (the results carry over), or run add_neighborhoods(obj, overwrite = TRUE) first to analyze the subset as a separate tissue.

Each kept cell already has its correct values, so you rarely need to recalculate. To treat the subset as a separate tissue instead, rebuild its neighborhoods first. This clears the carried-over tables, and the new values use only the kept cells:

separate <- add_neighborhoods(sub, overwrite = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
separate <- aggregate_NICHESObject(separate, verbose = FALSE)

Changing neighborhoods

add_neighborhoods(overwrite = TRUE) can also apply another edge.filter.mode. It clears existing aggregation tables, so run aggregation again afterward.

narrow <- add_neighborhoods(
  NICHESv2_example,
  edge.filter.mode = "central_cell_only",
  overwrite = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
narrow <- add_neighborhood_edge_agg(narrow, verbose = FALSE)
